newsitem.title: UK: UK firms lag international rivals in R&D spending.
newsitem.headline: UK firms lag international rivals in R&D spending.

text.p: Britain is lagging behind its international competitors in terms of corporate investment in research and development (R&D), according to a survey published on Thursday.
British firms increased R&D spending over the past five years, but their investment in R&D as a percentage of sales was still lower than that of the other top industrial countries.
Britain, along with Italy, spends only 2.3 percent of sales on R&D, compared with Japan's 4.9 percent, France's 4.0, Germany's 4.6 and the United States' 4.3.
"On this basis, the UK corporate sector is at the bottom of the league table...and it has not been improving relative to corporate sectors in most countries," the report said.

The UK R&D Scoreboard 1997, commissioned by Britain's Department of Trade and Industry, found that on a sector by sector basis major UK firms were investing at levels often well below the international average.

There were exceptions however, notably pharmaceuticals, where Britain's Glaxo Wellcome was top of the league in terms of R&D spending. Last year the firm spent 1.2 billion stg, or 13.0 percent of sales.
The report highlighted other British companies such as General Electric Co Plc, Rolls-Royce, Siebe, Unilever and Reuters, which were investing at levels matching their international peers.

Allen Yurko, chief executive of Siebe, who contributed to the report, said his company had found there was a direct correlation between the amount spend on R&D and long term growth rates of its competitors.
"Simply stated, more R&D means better growth and better profit," he said.

The report included 1997 rankings for the top 300 international firms by R&D expenditure. General Motors of the United States came top of the league, spending 5.2 billion stg, followed by Ford Motor Co with 3.9 billion, and then Siemens with 3.8 billion.
Glaxo Wellcome was the highest ranking British company, coming 23rd out of the 300.
